question: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe right shoulder pain and inability to move the shoulder for the past 30 minutes. The pain began after being tackled while playing football. He has nausea but has not vomited. He is in no apparent distress. Examination shows the right upper extremity externally rotated and slightly abducted. Palpation of the right shoulder joint shows tenderness and an empty glenoid fossa. The right humeral head is palpated below the coracoid process. The left upper extremity is unremarkable. The radial pulses are palpable bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.opc: Test sensation of the lateral shoulder

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Severe right shoulder pain after trauma" -> "Possible shoulder dislocation" -> "Tenderness and empty glenoid fossa on examination" -> "Humeral head palpated below coracoid process" -> "Indicates anterior shoulder dislocation" -> "Closed reduction is indicated" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Severe right shoulder pain after trauma" -> "Inability to move shoulder" -> "External rotation and slight abduction of arm" -> "Signs of anterior dislocation" -> "Closed reduction is the most appropriate next step" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Right shoulder pain and inability to move" -> "Physical exam shows empty glenoid fossa" -> "Humeral head displaced" -> "Suggests dislocation" -> "Immediate management requires closed reduction" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Right shoulder pain after being tackled" -> "Examination reveals dislocation signs" -> "Tenderness and abnormal positioning of humeral head" -> "Closed reduction is necessary to restore function" -> 80%
analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with an anterior shoulder dislocation, characterized by severe shoulder pain, inability to move the shoulder, and the position of the arm (externally rotated and slightly abducted). The empty glenoid fossa and palpation of the humeral head below the coracoid process further support this diagnosis. The most appropriate next step in management for an anterior shoulder dislocation is closed reduction, which is a standard procedure to restore the normal anatomy of the shoulder joint.
